title: One Calculator, Three Paradigms: Imperative, Functional and Object-Oriented Python
author: Michael Borck

courses.title: One Calculator, Three Paradigms: Imperative, Functional and Object-Oriented Python
courses.pitch: The same calculator built three ways, to make programming paradigms visible.

unit.title: One Calculator, Three Paradigms: Imperative, Functional and Object-Oriented Python
unit.pitch: The same calculator built three ways, to make programming paradigms visible.

blocks.html: A paradigm is a way of deciding what the code is made of.
The Concept First

The calculator does four things: add, subtract, multiply and divide. The behaviour is the same in every version. The structure is not.

The imperative version describes the steps: read input, choose an operation, compute, print, repeat. It uses functions and control flow, and the program is a sequence of actions.

The functional version treats operations as values. A dictionary maps menu choices to functions, and a higher-order function applies the chosen function. Pure functions do the arithmetic; the input and output remain impure at the edges.

The object-oriented version models the calculator as an object with state and behaviour. The Calculator owns the history; the Menu owns the interaction. The program is a set of collaborating objects.

None is the correct answer. Each makes a different thing easy to see:

  • imperative: the sequence and the state
  • functional: the operations and the data flow
  • object-oriented: the boundaries and the responsibilities
Understanding Through Three Recipes

Three cooks make the same soup. One writes a numbered procedure. One writes a set of transformations from ingredients to finished soup. One organises the kitchen into stations, each with its own tools and responsibilities.

The soup is the same. The kitchen is not.
Discovering Paradigms with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Name the Unit of Design

Ask the AI to identify the main building block in each version.

Here are three calculator implementations:
[paste them]

For each, name the main unit of design: the step, the function or the
object. Explain what that unit makes easy and what it hides.

A good answer will avoid ranking the paradigms and focus on the trade-off.

Exploration 2: Find the State

Ask where each version keeps changing data.

Where does each calculator keep its history or current state? Is it a
local variable, a returned value, a tuple, or an object attribute? What
does that choice make easier to test?

The functional version returns a new history; the object version mutates an attribute.

Exploration 3: Move a Feature

Ask what happens when you add a power operation.

Add a power operation to all three versions. Describe the change in each
and which files or functions it touches. Do not write the code.

The comparison is the lesson.
From Concept to Practice

A comparison table:

Question Imperative Functional Object-oriented
Main unit Step Function Object
State Variables Immutable values Attributes
Reuse Functions Higher-order functions Classes and composition
Test focus Paths Inputs and outputs Behaviour and collaborators
Risk Hidden coupling Abstraction overhead Over-engineering
Build Task
Run all three versions from the repository. Pick one feature and add it to two of them. Compare the diff.
Classroom Connection
The same problem in three styles is a strong assessment. A student who can explain the trade-off understands more than one who can only write the version they memorised.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 1.1 (Level 1). Name the main unit of design in each paradigm.

Exercise 1.2 (Level 2). Find where each version keeps state.

Exercise 1.3 (Level 3). Add a power operation to two versions and compare the diff.

Exercise 1.4 (Level 4). Explain which version is easiest to test and why.

Exercise 1.5 (Level 5). Choose a paradigm for a larger calculator and justify the choice.
Chapter Summary

• The same behaviour can have different structures.
  • Imperative, functional and object-oriented each make a different unit central.
  • The trade-off matters more than the ranking.
  • State placement changes testing.
  • The comparison is the lesson.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Ran all three versions
  • [ ] Named the main unit of each
  • [ ] Found the state
  • [ ] Added one feature
  • [ ] Explained a trade-off
Your Learning Journal

1. Which version felt most natural?
  2. Which was easiest to test?
  3. What did the other versions make visible?
Next Steps
The comparison is set. The next chapter reads the imperative version.
The imperative program tells the computer what to do, in order.
The Concept First

The imperative calculator has a main loop. It prints a menu, reads a choice, reads two numbers, calls calculate, prints the result and repeats.

The functions are small and readable:

def add(x, y):
    return x + y

def calculate(x, y, operation):
    if operation == "1":
        return add(x, y)
    elif operation == "2":
        return subtract(x, y)
    ...

The control flow is explicit. The state is local: choice, x, y and result. The loop is the program's spine.

The strength is directness. You can follow the program line by line. The weakness is coupling: adding an operation usually means editing the menu, the calculate chain and the input validation.
Understanding Through a Recipe

A recipe tells you to chop, heat, add, stir and wait. The order is the method.

The imperative calculator is a recipe. The steps are the design.
Discovering the Steps with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Trace One Run

Ask the AI to trace a single calculation.

Here is the imperative calculator:
[paste it]

Trace the run where the user chooses addition and enters 2 and 3.
List every function call, variable assignment and branch in order.

The trace shows the program's spine.

Exploration 2: Find the Coupling

Ask what changes when an operation is added.

Add a power operation to the imperative calculator. List every place
that must change: menu, input validation, calculate chain and tests.

The list is the cost of the design.

Exploration 3: Test the Edge

Ask where division by zero is handled and whether the message is good.

The divide function returns a string for division by zero. Explain what
the caller sees, whether the type changes, and how you would test it.

A string result in a numeric path is a design smell worth discussing.
From Concept to Practice

An imperative change record:

Change Files or functions
Add power Menu text, input validation, calculate chain, tests
Change menu main, read_input
Add history New list, print path, every operation
Validate number read_input only
Build Task
Add a power operation to the imperative version. Run it. Write down every place you changed.
Classroom Connection
The imperative version is the easiest starting point for beginners. It maps to the way a program executes: one step after another.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 2.1 (Level 1). Trace one addition run.

Exercise 2.2 (Level 2). Add a power operation.

Exercise 2.3 (Level 3). Improve the division-by-zero message.

Exercise 2.4 (Level 4). Add a history list and print it at exit.

Exercise 2.5 (Level 5). Refactor the operation choice to reduce coupling without changing behaviour.
Chapter Summary

• The imperative version is a sequence of steps.
  • The main loop is the spine.
  • State is local and explicit.
  • Adding an operation touches several places.
  • Directness is the strength; coupling is the cost.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Traced a run
  • [ ] Added one operation
  • [ ] Found the division edge
  • [ ] Counted the changes
  • [ ] Noticed one coupling
Your Learning Journal

1. Which step was easiest to follow?
  2. What did adding an operation cost?
  3. Where could the design be simplified?
Next Steps
The steps are clear. The next chapter treats operations as values.
The functional program treats functions as values and state as something you return.
The Concept First

The functional calculator defines pure arithmetic functions:

def add(x, y):
    return x + y

operators = {
    "1": add,
    "2": subtract,
    "3": multiply,
    "4": divide,
}

def calculate(x, y, func):
    return func(x, y)

The menu maps a choice to a function. calculate is a higher-order function: it takes another function as an argument.

The history is immutable. update_history returns a new tuple rather than appending to a list. The REPL is recursive rather than a while loop.

Input and output are still impure. That is honest: a program that talks to a person has side effects at the edges.

The strength is composition and testability. The arithmetic functions are pure. The weakness is that the style can feel abstract if the problem is simple.
Understanding Through a Factory Line

A factory line transforms materials. Each station is a function from input to output. The line is a composition of transformations.

The functional calculator is a small factory. The operations are the stations.
Discovering Functions with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Find the Pure Functions

Ask the AI to classify each function.

Here is the functional calculator:
[paste it]

Classify each function as pure or impure. Explain what makes it pure or
impure. Mark where the program must talk to the outside world.

The boundary is the lesson: pure inside, impure at the edges.

Exploration 2: Add an Operation

Ask what changes.

Add a power operation to the functional calculator. List the change in
the operators dictionary, the tests and any validation. Compare the
number of edits with the imperative version.

The functional version localises the operation.

Exploration 3: Test the History

Ask how immutability helps.

The history is a tuple returned by update_history. Explain how that
makes testing easier than a mutable list inside an object. What does it
cost?

The trade-off is memory and copying versus predictability.
From Concept to Practice

A functional change record:

Change Where
Add power One function, one dictionary entry
Test operation Call the pure function
History Return a new tuple
Input Impure edge
Build Task
Add a power function and one test. Do not change calculate. Explain why the change was local.
Classroom Connection
The functional version is a good introduction to higher-order functions, pure functions and immutable data. It also shows where purity stops: at the user.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 3.1 (Level 1). Classify each function as pure or impure.

Exercise 3.2 (Level 2). Add a power function.

Exercise 3.3 (Level 3). Test the arithmetic without input or output.

Exercise 3.4 (Level 4). Explain the immutable history.

Exercise 3.5 (Level 5). Refactor one impure edge into a pure function plus a thin wrapper.
Chapter Summary

• The functional version treats functions as values.
  • Pure functions are easy to test.
  • Immutability returns new data instead of changing it.
  • Input and output remain impure edges.
  • Composition is the strength; abstraction is the cost.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Found the pure functions
  • [ ] Added an operation
  • [ ] Tested one function
  • [ ] Explained the history
  • [ ] Found the impure edge
Your Learning Journal

1. Which function was easiest to test?
  2. Where did purity stop?
  3. Did the style make the problem clearer or harder?
Next Steps
The operations are values. The next chapter bundles state and behaviour.
The object-oriented program gives each thing a job and a boundary.
The Concept First

The object-oriented calculator has two classes:

  • Calculator owns the arithmetic and the history.
  • Menu owns the interaction.
class Calculator:
    def __init__(self):
        self.history = []

    def add(self, x, y):
        result = x + y
        self.history.append(("add", x, y, result))
        return result

The history is an attribute. Each operation mutates the object. The menu is a separate object with its own options and input handling.

The strength is responsibility. Each class has a boundary, and the main loop coordinates them. The weakness is that a small problem can carry more structure than it needs.
Understanding Through a Workshop

A workshop has stations: one for cutting, one for assembly, one for finishing. Each station has tools and a job. The supervisor coordinates the flow.

The object-oriented calculator is a small workshop. The classes are the stations.
Discovering Objects with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Find the Responsibilities

Ask the AI to list each class's job.

Here is the object-oriented calculator:
[paste it]

List the responsibility of each class and method. Mark any method that
does work belonging to another class.

A good answer will notice whether main knows too much.

Exploration 2: Add an Operation

Ask what changes.

Add a power operation to the object-oriented calculator. List the changes
in the class, the menu and the main dispatch. Compare the number of
edits with the functional version.

The object version localises the arithmetic but touches the menu and dispatch.

Exploration 3: Test the Object

Ask how to test the history.

Write three tests for Calculator: one for addition, one for division by
zero and one for the history. Do not use input() or print().

The object is testable without the menu.
From Concept to Practice

An object responsibility table:

Class Responsibility State
Calculator Arithmetic and history history
Menu Display and input options
main Coordinate the loop local variables
Build Task
Add a power method. Write one test for it. Then move one responsibility out of main into a class.
Classroom Connection
Objects are a natural way to teach boundaries and testability. The risk is over-design: not every problem needs a class hierarchy.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 4.1 (Level 1). List each class's responsibility.

Exercise 4.2 (Level 2). Add a power method.

Exercise 4.3 (Level 3). Test the calculator without the menu.

Exercise 4.4 (Level 4). Move one responsibility out of main.

Exercise 4.5 (Level 5). Decide whether this problem needs an object at all, and defend the answer.
Chapter Summary

• The object-oriented version gives each class a job.
  • State lives in attributes.
  • The menu is separate from the calculator.
  • Testability improves when the UI is separate.
  • Over-design is the risk.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Listed the responsibilities
  • [ ] Added an operation
  • [ ] Tested the object
  • [ ] Moved one responsibility
  • [ ] Judged the design
Your Learning Journal

1. Which boundary was clearest?
  2. Where did main know too much?
  3. Did the structure earn its cost?
Next Steps
The three versions are read. The final chapter compares them.
The paradigm is a tool for making a particular kind of change cheap.
The Concept First

The three calculators differ in where change is local:

  • Imperative: adding an operation touches the menu, validation and dispatch. The flow is obvious; the coupling is spread.
  • Functional: adding an operation touches one function and one dictionary entry. The arithmetic is pure and easy to test.
  • Object-oriented: adding an operation touches the class, the menu and the dispatch. The boundary is clear; the coordination remains.

The choice depends on the change you expect:

  • If the program is a sequence of steps, imperative is direct.
  • If the operations are the variability, functional composition is clean.
  • If the state and responsibilities are the variability, objects help.

The wrong question is "which paradigm is best?" The useful question is "what kind of change will this code face?"
Understanding Through Three Toolboxes

A hammer, a screwdriver and a wrench can all open a crate. The choice depends on the crate, the screw and the damage you want to avoid.

A paradigm is a toolbox. The job decides.
Discovering the Choice with Your AI Partner

Exploration 1: Predict the Change

Ask the AI to compare the cost of three future changes.

Compare the three calculators for these changes:
1. add a power operation
2. add a history feature
3. replace the text menu with a web form

For each, say which version is easiest to change and why.

The answer is a design judgement, not a ranking.

Exploration 2: Find the Test Boundary

Ask which version is easiest to test.

Compare the testability of the three versions. Which parts can be tested
without input, output or a running program? What does each design hide?

The functional arithmetic is easiest; the object boundary is next; the imperative flow needs more setup.

Exploration 3: Choose for a New Context

Ask for a recommendation.

A team expects frequent new operations and a web interface. Which
paradigm would you start with, and what would you borrow from the
others?

A good answer will combine ideas rather than pick a tribe.
From Concept to Practice

A decision record:

Context Likely choice Why
Teaching control flow Imperative Steps are visible
Many pure operations Functional Composition and tests
State and collaborators Object-oriented Boundaries and responsibilities
Mixed Hybrid Use each where it earns its place
Build Task
Write a short decision note for a calculator that will grow to twenty operations and a web UI. Name the paradigm and the trade-off.
Classroom Connection
The comparison is the assessment. A student who can explain why one version is easier to change has learned more than one who can recite definitions.
Practice Exercises

Exercise 5.1 (Level 1). Name one strength of each paradigm.

Exercise 5.2 (Level 2). Compare the cost of adding an operation.

Exercise 5.3 (Level 3). Compare testability.

Exercise 5.4 (Level 4). Choose a paradigm for a new context and justify it.

Exercise 5.5 (Level 5). Design a hybrid that borrows one idea from each version.
Chapter Summary

• The paradigm makes a kind of change cheap.
  • Imperative favours explicit flow.
  • Functional favours composition and pure functions.
  • Object-oriented favours state and responsibility boundaries.
  • Choose for the change you expect.
Reflection

Before moving on, ensure you:

  • [ ] Compared one change across all three
  • [ ] Compared testability
  • [ ] Chose for a context
  • [ ] Named a trade-off
  • [ ] Borrowed one idea from another paradigm
Your Learning Journal

1. Which change favoured each paradigm?
  2. Which version would you maintain?
  3. What would you borrow?
Next Steps
The comparison is complete. The playground has five katas if you want more practice.
